title: Terraform Plan & Apply: The Graph Under the Diff
summary: A deep field guide to what actually happens between `terraform plan` and `terraform apply` — how the dependency graph is built and walked, what refresh does to state, how to read every symbol in a plan diff, and when targeted apply and `-replace` are the right escape hatches.

chapters.title: Plan & Apply: The Core Model
points: Terraform is declarative convergence, not a script: you describe desired state, it computes the actions to reach it.
Plan has three inputs: configuration (HCL desired state), state file (prior known state), real infrastructure (read via refresh).
`terraform plan` is read-only — it never writes managed infrastructure and in modern versions never persists refreshed state.
`terraform plan -out=tfplan` saves a binary plan file; `terraform apply tfplan` applies exactly that, no re-plan, no approval prompt.
`terraform apply` with no plan file runs a plan internally and prompts `yes`; `-auto-approve` skips the prompt.
The saved plan file embeds the state snapshot it was based on — if state serial moved, apply fails with `Saved plan is stale`.
A plan file is NOT encrypted: it contains variable values and resource attributes including secrets. Never commit it.
`terraform plan -detailed-exitcode`: 0 = no changes, 1 = error, 2 = changes present. The standard CI drift gate.
Plan modes: normal, `-destroy` (plan the teardown), `-refresh-only` (propose state-only updates, no infrastructure change).
Apply is NOT a transaction — there is no rollback. A failed apply leaves partially created infrastructure recorded in state.
Idempotence test: a second apply immediately after the first must produce `No changes.` A non-empty plan means a perpetual-diff bug.
`terraform show -json tfplan` emits the stable machine-readable plan for policy engines (OPA/Conftest/Sentinel).
Example CI pipeline: `terraform plan -out=tfplan -detailed-exitcode` → artifact → policy check on JSON → `terraform apply tfplan`.
Plan output is a proposal, not a promise: unknown values may resolve at apply time to something the provider rejects.

chapters.title: The Dependency Graph (DAG)
points: Terraform builds a directed acyclic graph every run: nodes are resources, data sources, providers, variables, locals, outputs, modules.
Edges come from implicit references — writing `subnet_id = aws_subnet.a.id` creates an edge from the instance to the subnet.
`depends_on` adds an explicit edge for hidden dependencies (IAM policy that must exist before an instance uses it at runtime).
`depends_on` must be a static reference list — it cannot contain a computed expression.
The graph must be acyclic. `Error: Cycle: aws_security_group.a, aws_security_group.b` — usually mutual references or depends_on loops.
Fix cycles by splitting: use standalone `aws_security_group_rule` resources instead of inline mutually-referencing rules.
`terraform graph` prints DOT; pipe to Graphviz. `terraform graph -type=plan` shows the plan-time graph.
Create order = reverse topological order (dependencies first). Destroy order is inverted: dependents are destroyed before what they depend on.
Provider nodes are dependencies of every resource that uses them — a provider block configured from a resource attribute is a chicken-and-egg problem.
`count` and `for_each` are expanded during graph expansion: one node per instance, addressed `aws_subnet.this[0]` or `aws_subnet.this["a"]`.
Full address form: `module.network.aws_subnet.this["public-a"]` — module path, resource type, name, index key.
Data source nodes are read during plan when their arguments are known, and deferred to apply when they depend on unknown values.
`create_before_destroy` inverts the edge direction for that node pair so the new object exists before the old is removed.
`depends_on` on a `module` block applies to every resource inside that module — coarse, and it serializes the walk.
The graph walker runs independent nodes concurrently: default 10, tuned with `-parallelism=n`.
The graph is never persisted — it is rebuilt from config plus state on every plan and every apply.

chapters.title: State & Refresh
points: State maps config addresses to real object IDs plus the last-known attribute values — it is the only link between HCL and reality.
Refresh calls the provider's ReadResource for each managed resource, updating the in-memory state before the diff is computed.
Drift = a resource changed outside Terraform. Refresh detects it; the plan reports `Note: Objects have changed outside of Terraform`.
If a resource was deleted outside Terraform, refresh marks it gone and the plan proposes a create.
`terraform refresh` is deprecated (0.15.4+). Use `terraform plan -refresh-only` to inspect drift and `terraform apply -refresh-only` to accept it into state.
`-refresh=false` skips all reads: much faster, but plans against possibly stale attributes — an emergency speed flag, not a habit.
Refresh cost is O(number of resources) in API calls and dominates plan runtime on large root modules.
Data sources are not "refreshed" — they are re-evaluated from scratch on every plan.
Backends lock state for the duration of a write-capable run; `Error acquiring the state lock` means another run holds it.
`terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>` only when you are certain no apply is running — otherwise you invite concurrent writes and corruption.
Every state write increments the serial; the plan file records it, which is how staleness detection works.
State stores sensitive attributes in plaintext — use an encrypted backend (S3+SSE, Terraform Cloud) and restrict read access.
Surgical tools: `terraform state list`, `state show`, `state mv`, `state rm`, `terraform import`.
`import` blocks (1.5+) make imports declarative and reviewable; `plan -generate-config-out=gen.tf` scaffolds the HCL.
`moved` blocks preserve identity across refactors (renames, module extraction) instead of planning destroy + create.

chapters.title: Reading a Plan Diff
points: `+` create, `-` destroy, `~` update in place, `-/+` destroy then create (replace), `+/-` create then destroy (create_before_destroy), `<=` read data source.
Summary line is the headline: `Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 3 to destroy.` Read it before the body.
`# forces replacement` next to an attribute names the exact field that turned an update into a replacement.
`(known after apply)` marks an unknown — the provider computes it, so Terraform cannot show the final value.
One unknown poisons expressions downstream: an ID used inside a template makes the entire rendered string unknown and noisy.
`(sensitive value)` masks output; the value still exists in the plan file and in the JSON plan.
The `Note: Objects have changed outside of Terraform` block is drift, listed separately from planned actions — never scroll past it.
Replace reasons are printed: `will be replaced, as requested` (`-replace`), `is tainted, so must be replaced`, `has been deleted`.
No-op resources are hidden. Only changed resources appear under `Terraform will perform the following actions:`.
`Changes to Outputs:` is a separate trailing section — output-only diffs still count as changes.
`# module.db.aws_instance.this has moved to ...` shows `moved` block resolution with no infrastructure action.
In JSON: `resource_changes[].change.actions` is `["create"]`, `["update"]`, `["delete","create"]` (replace), `["create","delete"]` (CBD), or `["no-op"]`.
`replace_paths` in the JSON plan gives the machine-readable version of `# forces replacement`.
CI hygiene: `-no-color` and `-compact-warnings` keep logs readable; gate on `delete` actions against protected resource types.
Review discipline: scan for `must be replaced` and `will be destroyed` before reading anything else.

chapters.title: How a Plan Is Computed (Internals)
points: Provider plugin protocol calls, in order: GetProviderSchema, ValidateResourceConfig, ReadResource (refresh), PlanResourceChange, ApplyResourceChange.
PlanResourceChange receives three values per resource: prior state, proposed new state (config merged over prior), and config.
The provider — not Terraform core — decides whether a change is in-place or a replacement.
It signals replacement by returning `RequiresReplace` attribute paths, set via `ForceNew: true` (SDKv2) or `RequiresReplace()` plan modifiers (Plugin Framework).
Values are `cty` values; unknowns are a first-class value that propagates through every expression that touches them.
`Provider produced inconsistent final plan` means the applied value differed from a known planned value — a provider bug, not user error.
Diffing is whole-object: nested blocks and sets are compared elementwise, which is why set ordering changes can look like churn.
`lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags["LastModified"]] }` drops attributes from the diff; `ignore_changes = all` freezes everything after create.
`lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` makes any plan proposing destruction a hard error — including a `-replace`.
`precondition` / `postcondition` blocks assert invariants and fail the plan or apply with your own message.
`check` blocks run after apply and only warn — they never block the run.
A data source whose arguments are unknown is deferred to apply, so everything it feeds becomes unknown in the plan.
Provisioners are apply-time only; they never appear as detail in the plan, which is one reason they undermine plan review.
The plan file is an internal binary archive (plan + state snapshot); `terraform show -json` is the only stable contract for tooling.

chapters.title: Targeted Apply (`-target`)
points: `terraform apply -target=aws_instance.web` prunes the graph to that node plus everything it depends on.
Dependencies are pulled in automatically; dependents are excluded — the reverse of what people usually expect.
Repeat the flag for multiple targets: `-target=aws_instance.a -target=aws_instance.b`.
Module addresses work: `-target=module.vpc` targets every resource inside that module.
Indexed addresses need quoting: `-target='aws_instance.web[0]'` in bash, `-target="aws_instance.web[0]"` in PowerShell.
Terraform prints a warning every time: resource targeting is exceptional and the resulting state may be incomplete.
Outputs are not fully evaluated in a targeted run, so downstream consumers can read stale output values.
`-target` works on `plan`, `apply`, `destroy`, and `-refresh-only` — but it is a plan-time flag, so it cannot be applied to a saved plan file.
Targeting does not skip provider configuration or variable evaluation — required variables are still required.
Legitimate uses: recovering from a failed apply, working around a provider bug, breaking a chicken-and-egg bootstrap, fixing one drifted resource fast.
Illegitimate use: routine workflow. It hides broken configuration and produces state no full apply can reproduce.
Always follow a targeted apply with an untargeted `terraform plan` and confirm it converges to `No changes.`
Emergency fast loop: `terraform apply -target=... -refresh=false` skips the O(n) refresh entirely.
Newer Terraform versions add `-exclude` as the inverse — apply everything except the named addresses.
The real fix for chronic targeting is structural: split the root module so the blast radius matches the change.

chapters.title: Replace, Taint & Lifecycle
points: `terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web` forces destroy-then-create on a healthy resource — the modern way to "turn it off and on again".
`-replace` is plan-time: the replacement appears in a reviewable plan before anything happens.
`terraform taint` (deprecated in 0.15.2) mutated state out of band with no plan to review — that is why it was replaced.
`terraform untaint <address>` still exists to clear legacy tainted marks left by older workflows or failed creates.
Resources are tainted automatically when creation partially fails or a creation-time provisioner errors — the object exists but is not trustworthy.
`lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` builds the new object first; required for zero-downtime swaps.
create_before_destroy propagates: dependencies that must also be recreated inherit the flag, which is the usual source of surprising cascades.
Globally-unique names (S3 buckets, IAM roles) break under create_before_destroy unless you use `name_prefix` or a random suffix.
A deposed object is an old instance left behind when create_before_destroy's destroy step failed; it shows as `(deposed)` in the plan and is cleaned up on the next apply.
`prevent_destroy = true` blocks replacement too — you must remove the lifecycle block before `-replace` will run.
Update-in-place vs replacement is decided by the provider's schema, not by any user flag. `-replace` is the only user override.
`-replace` can be repeated and combined with `-target` for surgical recovery.
Replacement cascades: dependents that reference the replaced resource's computed attributes get their own updates or replacements.
To force downstream re-runs without a real replace, use `terraform_data` with `triggers_replace` (1.4+, the successor to `null_resource`).
Comparison — taint: state mutation, invisible until next plan, deprecated. `-replace`: plan-time, reviewable, reversible by not applying.

chapters.title: Apply Mechanics, Failure & Trade-offs
points: Apply walks the same DAG the plan produced, calling ApplyResourceChange per node in dependency order.
State is written incrementally as each resource completes — partial success is a normal outcome, not a corruption.
On error, Terraform lets in-flight nodes finish, stops scheduling new ones, persists state, and exits non-zero. Nothing is rolled back.
Recovery is always the same: re-run `terraform plan` and read what work remains.
If the state write itself fails, Terraform dumps `errored.tfstate` locally — recover with `terraform state push`.
`-parallelism=n` trade-off: raising it shortens wall-clock time but multiplies API rate-limit (429) and quota errors.
Per-resource `timeouts { create = "60m" }` blocks override provider defaults for slow resources like RDS or EKS.
Splitting plan and apply across CI jobs requires the same Terraform version, the same provider versions, the plan artifact, and an unchanged state serial.
`-auto-approve` is fine in CI only when the plan artifact was already reviewed or policy-checked; on a laptop it is how databases die.
Concurrent applies against one state are the primary corruption risk — state locking is the only guard, so never make `-lock=false` routine.
Plan runtime scales with resource count via refresh; the structural fix is smaller root modules, not faster flags.
Apply is not atomic across resources — design configurations so a re-run after failure is safe.
Provisioners and `local-exec` execute outside the plan/state model: they cannot be planned, diffed, or retried safely. Prefer `user_data` / cloud-init.
Trade-off summary: `-refresh=false` buys speed for accuracy, `-target` buys speed for completeness, high parallelism buys speed for rate-limit risk.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Gotchas
points: Perpetual diff: the provider normalizes a value (JSON policy whitespace, tag case, ARN casing) so config never matches state. Fix with `jsonencode()` or `ignore_changes`.
Making `-refresh=false` the default: fast plans that silently ignore real drift.
Using `-target` as a routine workflow — the config eventually only works when targeted.
Still reaching for `terraform taint` when `-replace` gives you a reviewable plan.
Applying a saved plan after someone else applied: `Saved plan is stale`. Re-plan; never work around it.
Committing `tfplan` or `terraform.tfstate` to git — both leak secrets in plaintext.
`depends_on` overuse: every extra edge serializes the graph and slows apply. Prefer real attribute references.
`count` index shift: removing the middle element of a list replaces every resource after it. Use `for_each` with stable string keys.
Switching `count` to `for_each` without `moved` blocks destroys and recreates the entire set.
Mutually referencing security groups create a cycle — split into standalone rule resources.
Skimming the plan and missing a `# forces replacement` on a stateful resource. Read every replacement line out loud.
Forgetting `prevent_destroy` on production data stores — and being surprised when it later blocks a legitimate `-replace`.
Ignoring the drift block: someone's console hotfix gets silently reverted by your next apply.
Treating the plan as a guarantee — `(known after apply)` values can resolve into something the API rejects mid-apply.
Running plan and apply on different Terraform or provider versions, so the applied diff is not the reviewed diff.
`force-unlock` on a lock held by a live apply — the fastest way to corrupt shared state.

chapters.title: Summary & Field Cheat Sheet
points: The loop, in order: build graph → refresh state via provider reads → diff config vs prior → provider plans each change → walk graph and apply.
`terraform plan -out=tfplan` then `terraform apply tfplan` is the only workflow where you apply exactly what you reviewed.
`-detailed-exitcode`: 0 no changes, 1 error, 2 changes — the drift-detection gate.
Diff symbols: `+` create, `-` destroy, `~` update, `-/+` replace, `+/-` create-before-destroy, `<=` data read.
`(known after apply)` = unknown; `# forces replacement` = the attribute that triggered a replace.
Drift lives in the `Objects have changed outside of Terraform` block; accept it with `apply -refresh-only`.
Graph edges come from references first, `depends_on` only for invisible runtime dependencies.
Cycles are config bugs — decompose the mutually-referencing resources.
`-target` includes dependencies, excludes dependents, warns loudly, and must always be followed by a clean full plan.
`-replace` supersedes `taint`; `create_before_destroy` for zero downtime; `prevent_destroy` for the resources you cannot lose.
Speed knobs and their cost: `-refresh=false` (accuracy), `-target` (completeness), `-parallelism` (rate limits). Structure beats all three.
Apply has no rollback and no cross-resource atomicity — state is written incrementally and re-running the plan is the recovery path.
Automate review, not approval: `terraform show -json tfplan` into a policy engine that fails on unexpected `delete` actions.
Health check for any module: apply twice; the second plan must say `No changes.`
